questions.stem: The EXCHANGE of oxygen and carbon dioxide between blood and air in the lungs occurs at the:

options.option_text: ALVEOLI — tiny sac-like structures with thin walls surrounded by pulmonary capillaries

questions.explanation: ALVEOLI (singular alveolus) — the tiny sac-like structures at the terminal end of the bronchial tree where actual GAS EXCHANGE takes place. STRUCTURE: ~300-500 MILLION alveoli in adult human lungs; combined surface area ~70-100 m² (equivalent to a badminton court — enables efficient exchange). Each alveolus is ~0.2-0.5 mm diameter; wall is a SINGLE-CELL-thick squamous epithelium (TYPE I pneumocytes); surrounded by a dense network of pulmonary capillaries. The alveolar-capillary barrier is only ~0.5 µm thick. MECHANISM: Oxygen diffuses DOWN its partial pressure gradient from alveolar air (PO₂ ~104 mmHg) into pulmonary capillary blood (PO₂ ~40 mmHg). CO₂ diffuses the other way (blood PCO₂ 45 → alveolar 40 mmHg). SURFACTANT — secreted by TYPE II pneumocytes; a phospholipid that reduces surface tension; prevents alveoli from collapsing on expiration. Deficient in premature babies → NEONATAL RESPIRATORY DISTRESS SYNDROME. PATHWAY of air: NOSTRIL → NASOPHARYNX → PHARYNX → LARYNX (voice box) → TRACHEA (windpipe, ~12cm) → 2 BRONCHI → BRONCHIOLES → TERMINAL bronchioles → RESPIRATORY bronchioles → ALVEOLAR DUCTS → ALVEOLI. Diseases that destroy alveoli: EMPHYSEMA (smoking), idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, ARDS.

questions.stem: The main muscle of respiration in humans is the:

options.option_text: DIAPHRAGM — a dome-shaped skeletal muscle separating thorax from abdomen; innervated by the phrenic nerve

questions.explanation: DIAPHRAGM — the primary muscle of respiration, a DOME-shaped skeletal muscle sheet separating the THORACIC cavity from the ABDOMINAL cavity. INNERVATION: PHRENIC NERVE (from cervical spinal roots C3, C4, C5 — 'C3-4-5 keeps the diaphragm alive' is a classic mnemonic; spinal cord injury ABOVE C3 = diaphragm paralysis = needs ventilator). MECHANISM: (1) During INSPIRATION — diaphragm CONTRACTS + flattens (moves down ~1-10 cm), EXTERNAL intercostals contract + lift the ribs UP + OUT, increasing thoracic volume → intra-thoracic pressure drops below atmospheric → air rushes in. (2) During EXPIRATION — diaphragm + intercostals RELAX, elastic recoil of lungs + chest wall reduces thoracic volume → pressure rises → air pushed out. Normal quiet expiration is PASSIVE. ACCESSORY muscles (used during exercise, breathlessness, asthma): sternocleidomastoid, scalenes (inspiration); abdominal + internal intercostals (forced expiration). HICCUPS = involuntary spasms of the diaphragm. LUNG VOLUMES: Tidal Volume (TV, normal breath) ~500 ml; Inspiratory Reserve Volume (IRV) ~3000 ml; Expiratory Reserve Volume (ERV) ~1100 ml; Residual Volume (RV, always stays in lungs) ~1200 ml. VITAL CAPACITY (VC) = TV + IRV + ERV ~4600 ml. TOTAL LUNG CAPACITY (TLC) = VC + RV ~5800 ml. Normal breathing rate = 12-20 breaths/min adult.

questions.stem: The protein in red blood cells that carries oxygen is:

options.option_text: HAEMOGLOBIN (Hb) — each tetramer carries up to 4 O₂ molecules; contains iron (Fe²⁺) in heme groups

questions.explanation: HAEMOGLOBIN (Hb) — the iron-containing oxygen-transport metalloprotein in the RED BLOOD CELLS (erythrocytes) of vertebrates. STRUCTURE: a TETRAMER of 4 polypeptide chains (2 ALPHA + 2 BETA in normal adult HbA). Each chain binds 1 HEME group → total 4 heme groups → can carry UP TO 4 O₂ MOLECULES per Hb. Each heme has an Fe²⁺ ion at centre that reversibly binds O₂. NORMAL LEVELS (adults): Male 13-17 g/dL; Female 12-15 g/dL. ANEMIA = low Hb. O₂ DISSOCIATION CURVE — SIGMOIDAL (S-shaped) — reflects cooperative binding; in lungs (high pO₂) Hb ~98% saturated; in tissues (low pO₂) drops O₂. BOHR EFFECT: high CO₂ / low pH shifts curve RIGHT (Hb releases O₂ more easily) — matches O₂ delivery to metabolically active tissue. CO (CARBON MONOXIDE) — binds Hb ~240× more tightly than O₂ → CARBOXYHEMOGLOBIN → tissue hypoxia → CO poisoning (kills silently; no colour/smell). HB TYPES: HbA (α2β2, adult); HbA2 (α2δ2, minor adult); HbF (α2γ2, fetal — higher O₂ affinity, pulls O₂ from maternal Hb across placenta); HbS (sickle — β6 glu→val mutation, sickle-cell disease). MYOGLOBIN — similar protein in MUSCLES (stores O₂ locally); monomer with 1 heme (hence 1 O₂); hyperbolic saturation curve. ERYTHROPOIETIN (EPO) — kidney hormone that stimulates RBC production.

questions.stem: MOST of the CO₂ in blood is transported as:

options.option_text: BICARBONATE (HCO₃⁻) in plasma — ~70% of CO₂ is carried this way, via the chloride shift in RBCs

questions.explanation: CO₂ TRANSPORT in blood — THREE forms, in approximately these proportions: (1) BICARBONATE (HCO₃⁻) in PLASMA — ~70% — the MAJOR form. Mechanism: in peripheral tissue, CO₂ diffuses into RBC → converted to H₂CO₃ by CARBONIC ANHYDRASE → dissociates to H⁺ + HCO₃⁻. H⁺ buffered by deoxyhemoglobin; HCO₃⁻ exits to plasma in exchange for Cl⁻ (CHLORIDE SHIFT / Hamburger phenomenon). In lungs, reverse happens. (2) CARBAMINOHAEMOGLOBIN (CO₂ bound to amino-terminal of globin) — ~23%. NOT same site as O₂ (which binds to heme Fe). (3) DISSOLVED CO₂ in plasma — ~7%. CARBONIC ANHYDRASE (CA) — zinc enzyme; catalyses CO₂ + H₂O ⇌ H₂CO₃ reaction 1000×s faster; abundant in RBCs. Inhibited by ACETAZOLAMIDE (used for glaucoma + altitude sickness). BOHR EFFECT: in actively metabolising tissue, ↑CO₂ + ↑H⁺ → Hb's O₂ affinity DROPS → releases more O₂ to the tissue. HALDANE EFFECT: in the lungs, when Hb binds O₂, it releases CO₂ + H⁺ → favours CO₂ exhalation. ACID-BASE: blood pH tightly regulated at 7.35-7.45. HCO₃⁻ is the main BUFFER. Hyperventilation → blows off CO₂ → RESPIRATORY ALKALOSIS; hypoventilation → RESPIRATORY ACIDOSIS. Kidneys compensate by adjusting bicarbonate excretion.

questions.stem: The air we EXHALE contains approximately what percentage of OXYGEN?

options.option_text: ~16-17% — still contains significant O₂ (enough that mouth-to-mouth resuscitation can work)

questions.explanation: COMPOSITION of INHALED vs EXHALED air (approximate percentages): | INHALED | EXHALED | CHANGE | Nitrogen (N₂) = 78% | 78% | ~0 | Oxygen (O₂) = 21% | ~16% | −5% | CO₂ = 0.04% | ~4% | +4% | Water vapor = variable | saturated (warm, moist) | ↑. KEY INSIGHT: exhaled air still has ~16% O₂ — enough to oxygenate another person's blood during MOUTH-TO-MOUTH resuscitation (CPR rescue breathing). CPR can maintain viability of brain tissue for 4-6 minutes until defibrillation/emergency care. NOBLE gases (argon, neon, etc.) ~1% — largely unchanged. AT REST: adult inhales ~6 L/min (tidal volume 0.5L × 12 breaths); consumes ~250 mL of O₂/min; produces ~200 mL of CO₂/min (so RER = 0.8). During EXERCISE: ventilation can rise 20-fold; O₂ consumption can rise from 250 mL/min to 4000 mL/min (16×) in elite athletes. PaO₂ (arterial partial pressure of O₂): normal 80-100 mmHg; SpO₂ (oxygen saturation, pulse oximetry): >95% normal; pulmonary physician alarm if SpO₂ <92%. High altitude / COVID-19 / asthma → low SpO₂. DEAD SPACE — volume of air that doesn't participate in gas exchange (trachea, bronchi) ~150 mL. OXYGEN CYLINDER colour code (India, ISO): WHITE (hospital pure O₂) — hence White Lung of the COVID era.

questions.stem: The RESPIRATORY CENTRE that controls breathing rhythm is located in the:

options.option_text: MEDULLA OBLONGATA + PONS (brainstem) — chemoreceptors monitor CO₂/pH + trigger involuntary breathing

questions.explanation: RESPIRATORY CONTROL — located in the BRAINSTEM (not cerebrum). KEY CENTRES: (1) MEDULLA OBLONGATA — contains the DORSAL RESPIRATORY GROUP (DRG, inspiration) + VENTRAL RESPIRATORY GROUP (VRG, expiration); drives basic rhythm. (2) PONS — contains PNEUMOTAXIC centre (limits inspiration duration) + APNEUSTIC centre (prolongs inspiration). CHEMORECEPTORS: (a) CENTRAL chemoreceptors in medulla — detect ↑H⁺ (i.e., ↑CO₂ indirectly via CSF) → most sensitive to hypercapnia → drive minute ventilation. (b) PERIPHERAL chemoreceptors in CAROTID BODIES (bifurcation of common carotid artery) + AORTIC BODIES — detect ↓O₂, ↑CO₂, ↓pH — drive breathing in hypoxia. CO₂ is the PRIMARY stimulus for normal breathing (not O₂!). This is why holding breath after HYPERVENTILATING is DANGEROUS — low CO₂ suppresses the drive to breathe, swimmer can black out underwater. IN COPD patients with chronic hypercapnia, they shift to HYPOXIC drive — giving them high-flow O₂ can suppress breathing (clinical caveat). VOLUNTARY control: cerebral cortex can override brainstem for speech, singing, breath-holding — but only up to a point; PaCO₂ rises + involuntary breathing resumes (you cannot suicide by holding your breath). HERING-BREUER REFLEX: stretch receptors in bronchi + bronchioles prevent over-inflation.

options.option_text: C-SHAPED rings of CARTILAGE (hyaline cartilage, ~16-20 rings) — keep airway open + allow oesophagus (behind) room to expand during swallowing

questions.explanation: TRACHEA (windpipe) — ~10-12 cm long, ~2-2.5 cm wide tube extending from the LARYNX (C6 vertebra) to its bifurcation at the CARINA (T4-T5) into left + right main bronchi. WALL: (a) 16-20 C-SHAPED rings of HYALINE CARTILAGE — prevent collapse during inspiration (high negative pressure). (b) OPEN POSTERIOR side filled with TRACHEALIS muscle + fibroelastic tissue — allows the OESOPHAGUS (which lies directly behind the trachea) to EXPAND FORWARD when swallowing a bolus. LINING: CILIATED PSEUDOSTRATIFIED COLUMNAR EPITHELIUM with GOBLET CELLS that secrete MUCUS. Cilia beat upward to push mucus + trapped debris up toward pharynx — the MUCOCILIARY ESCALATOR. Smokers' cilia are paralysed by nicotine → mucus pools → 'smoker's cough'. BIFURCATION: right main bronchus is WIDER, SHORTER + MORE VERTICAL than left → inhaled foreign bodies (peanuts, pins) more often lodge on the RIGHT. LEFT main bronchus more horizontal to pass under the aortic arch. Further branches: secondary (lobar) bronchi → tertiary (segmental) → bronchioles (<1mm, no cartilage) → terminal → respiratory → alveolar ducts → alveoli. TRACHEOSTOMY — surgical opening in trachea below the larynx, used for long-term ventilation.

options.option_text: MYCOBACTERIUM TUBERCULOSIS — a bacterium spread via airborne droplets; primarily affects lungs (pulmonary TB)

questions.explanation: TUBERCULOSIS (TB) — caused by the bacterium MYCOBACTERIUM TUBERCULOSIS, discovered by ROBERT KOCH on 24 MARCH 1882 (hence WORLD TB DAY on 24 March). TRANSMISSION: airborne droplets when an infected person coughs/sneezes. AFFECTS: primarily lungs (pulmonary TB) but can attack any organ (extra-pulmonary TB — lymph nodes, bones = Pott's disease of spine, meninges, kidneys). SYMPTOMS: chronic cough >2 weeks (often with blood — haemoptysis), night sweats, weight loss, fever, fatigue. DIAGNOSIS: SPUTUM AFB smear (Ziehl-Neelsen acid-fast stain — Mtb's waxy mycolic acid cell wall makes it 'acid-fast'), GeneXpert (molecular, rapid), CBNAAT, Mantoux (tuberculin skin test = latent TB), Chest X-ray (upper lobe cavitations). TREATMENT: COMBINATION THERAPY for 6 MONTHS — intensive 2-month phase with 4 drugs (RIPE — RIFAMPIN, ISONIAZID, PYRAZINAMIDE, ETHAMBUTOL) + continuation 4-month phase (RI). MDR-TB (multidrug-resistant, R+I resistant) + XDR-TB (extensively drug-resistant) harder to treat; BEDAQUILINE + DELAMANID new drugs. INDIA: has the HIGHEST TB BURDEN globally — ~26 lakh new cases/year; NATIONAL TB ELIMINATION PROGRAMME (NTEP, earlier RNTCP) aims for TB-FREE INDIA by 2025 (earlier than WHO's 2030 SDG target). NIKSHAY portal for reporting + tracking. Directly Observed Treatment Short-course (DOTS). BCG vaccine (given at birth, ~60-80% protective against severe childhood TB).

options.option_text: REVERSIBLE BRONCHOCONSTRICTION + airway inflammation + mucus hypersecretion — triggered by allergens, cold air, exercise

questions.explanation: ASTHMA — a CHRONIC INFLAMMATORY disease of the airways characterised by (a) REVERSIBLE bronchoconstriction (smooth muscle of bronchioles spasms), (b) airway inflammation (eosinophils, mast cells, lymphocytes), (c) mucus hypersecretion, (d) airway remodelling over years. SYMPTOMS: episodic wheezing, breathlessness, chest tightness, cough (often nocturnal). TRIGGERS: allergens (pollen, dust mites, animal dander), respiratory viruses, cold air, exercise, NSAIDs (aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease), smoke, GERD, emotional stress. PATHOPHYSIOLOGY: Type I HYPERSENSITIVITY (IgE-mediated) + Th2-dominant immune response → histamine + leukotrienes → bronchospasm. DIAGNOSIS: SPIROMETRY — ↓FEV1, ↓FEV1/FVC ratio, BUT REVERSIBLE with bronchodilator (>12% improvement). Peak expiratory flow rate (PEFR) variability. TREATMENT: (a) RELIEVERS — short-acting β2 agonists (SABA — SALBUTAMOL/ALBUTEROL 'blue inhaler'); (b) CONTROLLERS — inhaled CORTICOSTEROIDS (ICS — budesonide, fluticasone 'brown inhaler'), long-acting β2 (LABA — salmeterol), leukotriene receptor antagonists (MONTELUKAST), biologics (omalizumab for severe IgE-high). SEVERE ACUTE ATTACK ('status asthmaticus') — medical emergency; nebulised salbutamol + IV hydrocortisone + ipratropium + O₂ + magnesium sulfate. VS COPD: COPD is IRREVERSIBLE (smoking-induced), mostly older; ASTHMA is REVERSIBLE, often starts young, atopic. Global Burden: ~250 million asthmatics worldwide; ~35 million in India.

questions.stem: A HEALTHY adult's typical BREATHING RATE at rest is:
questions.explanation: RESPIRATORY RATE (breathing rate) by AGE at REST: (1) NEWBORN: 30-60/min (highest); (2) Infant (<1 yr): 30-40/min; (3) Toddler (1-3 yr): 24-40/min; (4) Preschool (3-5): 22-34/min; (5) School-age (6-12): 18-30/min; (6) Adolescent (12-18): 12-16/min; (7) ADULT: 12-20/min. TACHYPNEA = >20/min in adult; BRADYPNEA = <12/min. PATHOLOGICAL fast breathing: fever, pneumonia, asthma attack, metabolic acidosis (Kussmaul breathing in DKA), pain, anxiety, sepsis, PE. PATHOLOGICAL slow breathing: opioid overdose, sedatives, raised intracranial pressure, hypothyroidism, severe hypothermia. TIDAL VOLUME (TV) ~500 mL per breath; MINUTE VENTILATION = TV × RR = ~6-8 L/min at rest; can rise to 100-150 L/min in exercise (elite athletes up to 200). CHEYNE-STOKES RESPIRATION: alternating apnea + hyperpnea — seen in heart failure, stroke, approach to death. KUSSMAUL BREATHING: deep + fast — metabolic acidosis (DKA). NORMAL pulse oximetry SpO₂: >95%. During EXERCISE: RR rises via central command + peripheral receptors + CO₂ production; O₂ delivery can increase 16×. Elite athletes have resting RR as low as 8-10/min (more efficient). Yogic PRANAYAMA practices aim to slow + deepen breathing (heart rate + sympathetic tone).
